metric.why: Idle servers burn power, licenses, and depreciation while producing nothing. Fleet utilization is where the money hides in most enterprise estates, and it is the denominator that makes every efficiency metric honest.
metric.definition: The share of provisioned compute doing real work, measured over time rather than at peak.

reading.body:
Server utilization rate measures the share of provisioned compute doing real work over time rather than at peak, and it is the denominator that makes every efficiency claim honest.

Idle capacity is not free. Idle servers burn power, licenses, and depreciation while producing nothing, so a fleet measured at peak can look fully used while much of its cost buys no output. Measuring over time rather than at peak is what exposes the gap.

The category places utilization beside two physical constraints, stranded power and space per cabinet, and floor loading limits. These describe one question from three sides. Utilization says how much installed compute is working. Stranded power and space says how much of the building is provisioned but unusable. Floor loading says how much more equipment the structure can carry. A utilization figure alone cannot tell you whether a site has room to grow, because a fully used fleet in a building with no spare power or floor capacity is still at its limit.

The definition comes with no utilization value, fleet size, time series, or breakdown by operator or workload. It establishes what to measure and why, not the condition of any real fleet. A reader cannot conclude from it whether AI data centers run hot or cold. They can conclude that the question is the right one, and that it is a question about power and buildings as much as about servers.
